common_name: Revolute Daylily (1953 Stout Medal Tall Yellow Diploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Revolute's exceptionally tall scapes benefit from a sheltered spot away from strong winds.

directions: Hybridized by H.P. Sass and introduced in 1944, Revolute went on to earn the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 1953 for its clear, medium-yellow, trumpet-shaped flowers held on exceptionally tall, sturdy scapes that tower well above the clump. Its height and vigor made it a favored parent in mid-century breeding programs aimed at combining tall, well-branched scapes with clean, unmarked color. The dormant foliage dies back fully in winter, and clumps multiply steadily without becoming aggressive. Plant in full sun in average garden soil and divide every four to five years once flowering begins to taper off.
sources: K-State Gardens Stout Silver Medal Collection

common_name: Ruffled Pinafore Daylily (1957 Stout Medal Melon Diploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; the rosy-haloed melon blooms show their best color in full sun rather than partial shade.

directions: Bred by Milliken and introduced in 1948, Ruffled Pinafore won the Stout Silver Medal in 1957 for its light melon flowers softly overlaid with a rosy halo near the petal edges, a subtle bicolor effect that was novel among daylilies of its era. The ruffled petal margins referenced in its name give each bloom a dressy, textured look rather than a flat, smooth face. It forms a dependable dormant clump that increases at a moderate rate and holds its color well through summer heat. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil and divide congested clumps every three to four years.
sources: K-State Gardens Stout Silver Medal Collection

common_name: Salmon Sheen Daylily (1959 Stout Medal Reblooming Diploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; expect an early main bloom flush followed by a useful rebloom later in the season.

directions: Hybridized by B. Taylor and introduced in 1950, Salmon Sheen earned an Award of Merit in 1956 before going on to claim the Stout Silver Medal in 1959, prized for its red-orange, bitone-to-polychrome flowers carried on slender, gently curving scapes that sway in even a light breeze. It is an early bloomer that also throws a useful later flush of rebloom in favorable seasons, extending color beyond the main early-summer display. The evergreen foliage tolerates a bit of filtered shade, though flower color stays more saturated in full sun. Divide the fast-multiplying clumps every two to three years to keep bloom counts high.

common_name: Playboy Daylily (1961 Stout Medal Orange Diploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Playboy's clean orange color and evergreen foliage suit warmer-winter gardens especially well.

directions: Hybridized by Wheeler, Playboy received the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 1961 for its clean, unpatterned orange flowers that open in a single, non-double form measuring more than four and a half inches across. It blooms in the early midseason window and holds its color through summer heat without fading to a duller tone. The evergreen foliage stays attractive into fall in milder climates, and the diurnal flowers open fresh each morning with no notable fragrance. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and divide clumps every three to four years to sustain vigorous flowering.
sources: K-State Gardens Stout Silver Medal Collection

common_name: Multnomah Daylily (1963 Stout Medal Apricot-Pink Diploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Multnomah's compact, two-foot habit fits well near the front of mixed perennial borders.

directions: Hybridized by Kraus and introduced in 1954, Multnomah was awarded the Stout Silver Medal in 1963 for its apricot flowers softly overlaid with pale pink, a delicate blended tone that stood out among the brighter self-colors common at the time. The diploid plant forms a compact, well-mannered clump about two feet tall, well suited to smaller borders where taller mid-century daylilies would overwhelm the scale. Its dormant foliage dies back cleanly each fall, and clumps increase at a steady, easily managed pace. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and divide every three to four years.
sources: K-State Gardens Stout Silver Medal Collection

common_name: Full Reward Daylily (1967 Stout Medal Yellow Diploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Full Reward holds its cadmium-yellow color well even during peak summer heat.

directions: Bred by McVicker-Murphey and introduced in 1957, Full Reward earned the Stout Silver Medal in 1967 for its clear, cadmium-yellow self flowers held on tall, well-proportioned scapes that rise cleanly above the foliage clump. Unlike some yellow daylilies of its generation that faded or bleached in strong sun, Full Reward was noted for holding its saturated color through the heat of the day. The dormant, diploid plant multiplies at a moderate rate and forms a tidy, upright clump. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years once flowering slows.
sources: K-State Gardens Stout Silver Medal Collection

common_name: Satin Glass Daylily (1968 Stout Medal Pale Melon Diploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Satin Glass's pale melon flowers show their cool green throat best in bright light.

directions: Hybridized by Fay and Hardy and introduced in 1960, Satin Glass received the Stout Silver Medal in 1968 for its pale, melon-yellow flowers set off by a cool green throat, a soft, luminous combination that gave the cultivar its name. The tall, dormant diploid plant carries its blooms well above the foliage on sturdy scapes that hold up cleanly through summer storms. It increases at a dependable pace without crowding itself too quickly. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and divide congested clumps every three to four years.
sources: K-State Gardens Stout Silver Medal Collection

common_name: Hortensia Daylily (1972 Stout Medal Yellow Diploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Hortensia's tall scapes and large yellow flowers make a strong midsummer focal point.

directions: Bred by Branch and introduced in 1964, Hortensia was awarded the Stout Silver Medal in 1972 for its five-inch, clear yellow self flowers accented by a cool green throat and carried on tall scapes that hold the blooms well clear of the clump. The dormant, diploid plant is vigorous and increases steadily, forming a substantial clump within a few growing seasons of division. Its unmarked yellow color and generous flower size made it a benchmark for later yellow diploid breeding programs. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil and divide every three to four years to maintain strong bloom counts.
sources: K-State Gardens Stout Silver Medal Collection

common_name: Moment of Truth Daylily (1979 Stout Medal Near-White Diploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Moment of Truth's near-white flowers show cleanest color out of intense afternoon sun in hot climates.

directions: Hybridized by MacMillan and introduced in 1969, Moment of Truth earned the Stout Silver Medal in 1979 for its near-white, six-inch self flowers, a color class daylily breeders had long struggled to achieve cleanly on a compact plant. Its evergreen foliage persists through mild winters, giving the clump a tidier year-round presence than the dormant near-white daylilies that preceded it. The plant stays a modest two feet tall, making it easy to place near the front of a border. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil and divide every three to four years as clumps become crowded.
sources: K-State Gardens Stout Silver Medal Collection

common_name: Alabama Jubilee Daylily (Fragrant Red-Orange Tetraploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Alabama Jubilee's fluorescent red-orange color intensifies in strong sunlight.

directions: Hybridized by Webster and introduced in 1988, Alabama Jubilee produces fluorescent red-orange, seven-inch flowers rimmed with an even brighter red halo, a hot-toned combination that has kept it a steady nursery best-seller for decades. This tetraploid daylily is fragrant, blooms in midseason on scapes about thirty inches tall, and earned an Honorable Mention from the American Hemerocallis Society. The dormant foliage dies back cleanly in winter, and clumps build vigorously once established. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years.

common_name: Chicago Star Daylily (Fragrant Yellow Tetraploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Chicago Star is part of the widely grown Chicago series of tetraploid daylilies.

directions: Bred by Marsh and introduced in 1970 as part of the well-known Chicago series of tetraploid daylilies, Chicago Star bears large, clear yellow flowers up to eight inches across on compact scapes that keep the plant from looking top-heavy. It is fragrant, blooms in midseason, and earned an Honorable Mention from the American Hemerocallis Society on its way to becoming one of the series' most widely sold members. The semi-evergreen foliage holds up in a broad range of climates from the Upper Midwest into the Deep South. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Dublin Elaine Daylily (Peachy-Pink Double Rebloomer)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Dublin Elaine's double peachy-pink blooms rebloom later in the season than many everblooming cultivars.

directions: Hybridized by Joiner and introduced in 1987, Dublin Elaine carries fully double, peachy-pink flowers about five and a half inches across on scapes reaching roughly thirty-two inches, and it reblooms vigorously enough to have earned recognition as an All-American Daylily Selection along with an Award of Merit. Its rebloom cycle tends to run later in the season than many rebloomers, giving gardeners fresh color once earlier-flowering cultivars have finished. The dormant foliage dies back fully each winter, and the clump builds strength quickly after division. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years.

common_name: Indian Giver Daylily (Purple White-Edged Rebloomer)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Indian Giver's purple color deepens in full sun and lightens noticeably in partial shade.

directions: Bred by Ferguson and introduced in 1991, Indian Giver bears purple, four-and-a-half-inch flowers outlined by a thin, crisp white edge, a color pattern that shifts from lighter purple in shade to a deeper tone in full sun. It blooms early to midseason and reblooms reliably through the rest of the summer, a combination that earned it an Award of Merit from the American Hemerocallis Society. The compact, twenty-inch scapes keep the flowers close to the foliage clump, suiting front-of-border placement. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil and divide every three to four years to sustain heavy rebloom.

common_name: Kansas Kitten Daylily (Fragrant Lavender-Purple Rebloomer)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Kansas Kitten reblooms off and on through summer once the main flush finishes.

directions: Hybridized by Trimmer and introduced in 2010, Kansas Kitten produces fragrant, lavender-purple flowers about five inches across, each centered with a distinctly darker purple eye that sharpens the bicolor effect. It blooms in midseason and continues sending up scapes off and on through the rest of summer, a rebloom habit that helped it earn an Honorable Mention. Though registered as dormant, the clump has proven adaptable well beyond its official cold-hardiness rating in field trials. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years.

common_name: Lady Georgia Daylily (Peachy Apricot Reblooming Tetraploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Lady Georgia's soft apricot tone works well in pastel-themed borders.

directions: Hybridized by Dallas Jent, Lady Georgia bears soft, peachy-apricot flowers about five inches across on scapes near thirty inches tall, opening early in the season and continuing to rebloom through summer. This tetraploid daylily's gentle, cooling color reads less hot than many apricot cultivars bred for maximum saturation, making it easy to blend into pastel borders. The semi-evergreen foliage carries reasonably well into fall in milder zones. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years to keep bloom counts strong.

common_name: Lady Lucille Daylily (Deep Orange Reblooming All-American Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Lady Lucille's intense orange color holds up well into the heat of midsummer.

directions: Bred by Yvonne Enck, Lady Lucille produces intensely colored, six-inch orange flowers with petals darker than the sepals and a deeper orange blush radiating from the throat along a prominent yellow midrib. It blooms mid to late season and reblooms strongly enough through the rest of summer to have been named an All-American Daylily Selection. The dormant clump stays a manageable two feet tall, keeping the bold flower color from overwhelming smaller garden beds. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years.

common_name: Lullaby Baby Daylily (Fragrant Near-White Rebloomer)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Lullaby Baby's light fragrance is most noticeable in the cool of early morning.

directions: Hybridized by W. Spaulding and introduced in 1975, Lullaby Baby bears small, lightly fragrant, near-white flowers about three and a half inches across on compact nineteen-inch scapes, blooming early to midseason with a dependable later encore. Its combination of fragrance, rebloom, and pale color earned it the Lenington All-American Award along with an Award of Merit, and it remains a recognized All-American Daylily Selection decades after its introduction. The semi-evergreen foliage stays neat through most of the growing season. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil and divide every three to four years to sustain vigorous rebloom.

common_name: Miss Amelia Daylily (Fragrant Near-White Long-Season Rebloomer)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Miss Amelia is grown primarily for its unusually long rebloom season.

directions: Hybridized by Rick Ellinger, Miss Amelia produces pale yellow flowers that read almost white from a distance, each about three and a half inches across and lightly fragrant, on scapes reaching roughly thirty inches. It opens its first flowers early in the season and is known for exceptionally long rebloom, often continuing to flower for more than one hundred days in a single growing season. The semi-evergreen foliage holds up well across a range of climates. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years to keep the extended rebloom cycle strong.

common_name: Persian Ruby Daylily (Dark Red Spider-Form Tetraploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Persian Ruby's massive spider-form blooms benefit from a wind-sheltered spot.

directions: Bred by Trimmer and introduced in 1998, Persian Ruby carries huge, spider-form flowers nearly eight inches across in a deep, dark ruby-red set off by a large golden throat, a scale and color combination that earned it the American Hemerocallis Society's Extra-Large Bloom Award along with an Award of Merit. This tetraploid daylily blooms early to midseason on scapes about thirty inches tall, strong enough to hold the outsized flowers upright even after rain. The dormant foliage proves surprisingly cold-hardy for a variety of its size and color depth. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years.

common_name: Pooh Bear Daylily (Fragrant Gold Burgundy-Eyed Tetraploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Pooh Bear's burgundy-edged gold blooms rebloom steadily through summer.

directions: Hybridized by Darrel Apps, Pooh Bear bears gold flowers about four and a half inches across accented by a burgundy eye and a matching burgundy edge, a crisp two-tone combination on a lightly fragrant, tetraploid bloom. It opens early to midseason and continues reblooming through summer, quickly becoming a popular nursery-trade introduction. The semi-evergreen foliage stays tidy on scapes reaching about thirty-two inches. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil and divide every three to four years as the clump fills in.

common_name: Wayside King Royale Daylily (Fragrant Deep Purple Tetraploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Wayside King Royale needs a period of winter chill to perform at its best.

directions: Hybridized by Klehm and Elsley and introduced in 1987, Wayside King Royale bears deep purple, six-inch flowers on tall, thirty-six-inch scapes, with a fragrance and color saturation that holds up unusually well through summer heat rather than fading toward blue or gray. It blooms early to midseason and has remained a steady nursery favorite for its richly colored, weather-resistant flowers. The dormant foliage requires a period of winter chill to perform its best, suiting it to colder climates than many modern tetraploids. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years.
